# Brief — the idea (rev 3, after idea-review 1 and its re-review)

## Question
When a trained tabular model's prediction is "justified" by one run of a randomised SHAP estimator under a deployment-sized budget, **for which instances, models, datasets and budgets is that one run a reliable basis for the conclusions a reader draws from it** (which features are top, in what order, with which sign) — and can the user *know* this from the single run alone?

Not "is SHAP noisy?" (at low budget it is) but: where does the noise change a **decision-relevant conclusion**, against what yardstick, and can the run certify itself.

## What prior work leaves open
- Estimator papers (Kernel SHAP, unbiased Kernel SHAP + variance estimates, permutation / antithetic sampling, Leverage SHAP, regression-adjusted MC, SHAP-IQ) report error to the exact Shapley value, mostly L2, averaged over instances, at chosen budgets. Top-k *identification* is treated from the algorithm-design side (Shapley bandits, antithetic top-k sampling), with guarantees, not as a measurement of deployed default estimators on real models.
- Disagreement / robustness / LIME-stability work compares *methods* or perturbed inputs; the repeat-run variability of one explainer on one fixed model+instance is not separated from method, background, or retraining.
- Background-size stability (Yuan et al.) is deep-model only and does not separate sampling noise from the change of the value function.
- Rashomon / multiplicity work gives a natural yardstick (variability between equally accurate retrained models) but has not been used to calibrate explainer noise.

## Contributions, ranked
**Main (the paper's result must survive on these alone):**
1. **Exact-reference protocol.** Error is measured to the Shapley value of the *same* value function (same background rows, same output space, same feature unit), so explainer randomness is separated from the definition of the attribution; and the paper reports *which part of the pipeline is random* (e.g. shap's Kernel SHAP at 2d+2048 samples enumerates the extreme coalition sizes exactly and samples only the rest; for d ≤ 10 the default is fully exact; for a linear model with marginal value function the estimator has zero variance — a built-in negative control).
2. **A map of conditions**: top-k reliability as a function of budget, estimator, model family, d, and the exact attribution margin of the instance — with the answer allowed to be "reliable", "conditional" or "unreliable".
**Means:** 3. decision-relevant metrics and noise floors (below).
**Risky, may be a negative result and must not carry the paper:** 4. a single-run check (within-run variance + estimated margin) for top-k instability and a minimum-budget rule; compared against the trivial competitor "run twice and compare".

## Fixed definitions (pre-registered before experiments; results may change a *reading*, not these choices; sensitivity reported)
- **Players / feature unit:** original raw attributes; a categorical attribute is one player (one-hot encoded inside the model wrapper). German Credit d=20; ACS tasks use their own raw columns.
- **Value function:** marginal (interventional) with a fixed background of B_def = 50 rows drawn once per (dataset, seed) from the training set; the background is part of the *definition* and held fixed in all explainer-noise experiments. Budget is stated as coalition samples m (model evaluations = m × B_def).
- **Output space** (same for exact and estimated values): LR and MLP → log-odds; GBM → raw margin (log-odds); RF → class-1 probability (the output TreeSHAP explains). Rankings in other spaces are not claimed, and **cross-family comparisons in the map mix model class with output space**, so they are not claimed as such; as a check, RF is also explained in log-odds on the cells where that is feasible on the Kernel SHAP side (E1 cells) and compared with the probability-space result.

# How the study relates to prior work

**Shapley attribution and its estimators.** SHAP (Lundberg & Lee 2017) casts feature attribution as Shapley values of a
value function defined by removing features; the value function can be marginal or conditional
(Chen et al. 2020; Sundararajan & Najmi 2020; Kumar et al. 2020; Covert et al. 2020 unify removal-based explanations).
Model-agnostic estimation is randomised: Kernel SHAP and its unbiased variant with variance/convergence estimates
(Covert & Lee 2021), permutation / antithetic sampling (Mitchell et al. 2022), Leverage SHAP with guarantees
(Musco & Witter 2025), regression-adjusted MC (Witter et al. 2025), SHAP-IQ (Fumagalli et al. 2023); an overview in Chen et al. 2023.
Trees admit deterministic TreeSHAP (Lundberg et al. 2020). These works measure error to the exact Shapley value
(typically L2, averaged over instances, at chosen budgets). **Gap:** whether one run at a deployment budget supports the
decision-relevant conclusions drawn from it, instance by instance, is not studied; nor whether the run can detect its own failure.

**Rank / top-k identification.** The question "does the estimated order of players give the right top-k" is asked from the estimator side: Shapley bandits for top-k identification (Kolpaczki et al. 2021) and antithetic sampling for top-k Shapley identification (2025). Those design algorithms with sampling guarantees; we *measure* deployed default estimators on real tabular models, map the conditions (budget, model, d, instance margin) and test whether the run can flag its own failure. Covert & Lee 2021 already give within-run variance and convergence detection, so the novelty of the check is its validation against the top-k conclusion, not the variance estimate. Huang & Marques-Silva 2023 (inadequacy of Shapley values) is cited only to bound scope: we hold the Shapley value function fixed. ShapleyVIC (Rashomon-style Shapley importance across near-optimal models) is related to our retrain yardstick.

**Explanation disagreement and robustness.** Krishna et al. 2022 and Neely et al. 2021 study disagreement *between* methods;
Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola 2018 and Ghorbani et al. 2019 study sensitivity to input perturbation; Visani et al. 2022 study LIME stability
under resampling; Yuan et al. 2022 study background size for deep models. **Difference:** we fix model, value function and instance
and isolate the explainer's own randomness against an exact reference, and compare it to background and retraining noise.

input:
cat > paper/related.tex <<'EOF'
\paragraph{Shapley attribution and its estimators.}
SHAP casts feature attribution as the Shapley value of a value function that removes features \citep{lundberg2017}; the value function may be marginal or conditional \citep{chen2020,sundararajan2020,kumar2020}, and removal-based explanations share this structure \citep{covert2020removal}.
Model-agnostic estimation is randomised: Kernel SHAP and its unbiased variant with variance and convergence estimates \citep{covert2021}, permutation and antithetic sampling \citep{mitchell2022}, Leverage SHAP with guarantees \citep{musco2025}, regression-adjusted Monte Carlo \citep{witter2025regadj} and SHAP-IQ \citep{fumagalli2023}; \citet{chen2023algorithms} survey the algorithms.
Tree ensembles admit a deterministic algorithm \citep{lundberg2020trees}.
These works report the error to the exact Shapley value, usually in $\ell_2$ and averaged over instances, at chosen budgets.
They do not ask whether one run at a deployment budget supports the conclusion a reader draws from it for a given instance, nor whether the run can detect its own failure.

\paragraph{Top-$k$ identification.}
Whether an estimated ordering yields the right top-$k$ is asked from the estimator side: Shapley bandits for top-$k$ identification \citep{kolpaczki2021bandits} and antithetic sampling for top-$k$ Shapley identification \citep{antitheticTopK2025} design algorithms with sampling guarantees.
We instead measure deployed default estimators on trained tabular models and map the conditions under which one run identifies the right features.
\citet{covert2021} already give within-run variance and convergence detection, so what we add to the single-run check is its validation against the top-$k$ conclusion.
\citet{huang2023} question what Shapley values say about a model; we only bound scope by holding the value function fixed.

\paragraph{Disagreement and robustness.}
\citet{krishna2022} and \citet{neely2021} study disagreement between explanation methods; \citet{alvarez2018} and \citet{ghorbani2019fragile} study sensitivity to input perturbation; \citet{visani2022lime} study LIME stability under resampling; \citet{yuan2022} study background size for deep models.
We fix the model, the value function and the instance, and isolate the explainer's own randomness against an exact reference, then compare it with background and retraining noise.

\paragraph{Multiplicity as a yardstick.}
Predictive multiplicity and the Rashomon set \citep{marx2020,fisher2019,dong2020cloud} give the variability between equally accurate models; ShapleyVIC \citep{shapleyvic2022} applies this to Shapley importance.
We use it as a noise floor for explainer noise, not as the target.

\paragraph{Metrics and data.}
We measure the stability of selected sets with the index of \citet{nogueira2018} and the agreement of rankings with rank-biased overlap \citep{webber2010}.
The data are German Credit, the ACS tasks of \citet{ding2021}, and other public tabular sets (Section~\ref{sec:design}); tabular deep models follow \citet{gorishniy2021}.
EOF
